doc.title: Kenny Davern interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 16, 2001 [interview 2 of 2]

title: The Salty Dogs, 'Nixieland' and the Goon Shows
summary: He describes playing New Orleans revival music with the Salty Dogs while at Nick's, around 1957-58, and listening to Goon Shows.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: That’s good, Wow. Who are the Salty Dogs?

Well it was made up of a group of guys who had the oldest traditional, longest lived traditional band going in New York City at that time, which was basically the Red Onion jazz band. They are a group of scholars, you know, I mean they taught, they were Columbia professors and stuff like that. And they played because they loved music. They loved the King Oliver band or they loved the New Orleans Rhythm Kings you see. And at that time I was going through a learning process, or re-learning, or un-learning process of wanting to explore the possibilities of well what were those New Orleans guys, what did it feel like to play hymns and stuff like that. And I had a group of guys who also loved the same kind of music that I did. And at that time I was playing at Nick’s in Greenwich Village, and we used to be called the slick Italian Dixieland band you know. Nixieland band.

Yeah it’s called Nixieland music. And this was like our sort of version of a New Orleans revival band that was happening in Britain at that time, Monty Sunshine and Chris Barber and all those guys, Kenny Ball, big hits they had over there, and here too, “Midnight in Moscow” or stuff like that. And so this was about ’57 or ’58. And we had our own little band and we did this same kind of feel, and we played you know like country clubs playing old Gospel music, kind of hymns. “Lord, Lord, Lord you shore been good to me,” “Walking with the King,” “Just a Little While to Stay Here.” That they still make a career of in New Orleans now. I mean it’s so hokey it’s ridiculous. But we wanted it just, at that time. And I would take the recordings I had, you know Wooden Joe Nicholas and “Night at Artesian Hall” with Albert Burbank and Big Jim Robinson, Baby Dodds, and play it for the guys that I was working with, and it was very, very esoteric, well done, well played Nixieland band. We really played those classic jazz band things to a turn. And this was really rough music. I played it for these guys and they all looked like I was crazy. “You like that shit?” “Yeah I love it.” Oh man. But at the same time I used to listen to The Goon Shows on WBAI. And I was roaring with laughter, not really © Fillius Jazz Archive -12-
understanding what they were even saying, but the way the rhythm was so good with Sellers and company, you know The Goon Show. Did you ever hear any of those?

No. Dudley Moore was not on that. He was in the crowd but he wasn’t one of those guys. This was Spike Milligan and what else. Well at any rate, they used to broadcast those things from London. And I thought they were the funniest things I ever heard in my life. And they would listen to that and they looked at me like I’m nuts. Crazy. So I played them these records, “That’s awful.” Well anyway that’s what it was about. That was the Salty Dogs. We have one record we left testament.
